title: Give the marker a mark scheme
allegory: An LLM scorer is like a hired exam marker who is fast and usually agrees with you, but without a mark scheme rewards neat, long, confident scripts, so you give them anchored grade descriptors and sample scripts, make them write the comment before the mark, and re-mark the top and bottom scripts yourself.
map: a strong LLM grading each generated question
the mark scheme: what a 0, a 50 and a 100 look like
a rubric with a fixed range and anchored endpoints and midpoint
sample scripts, including a confident wrong one marked low
the comment written before the mark
an explanation first, then the integer score in SCORE tags
re-marking the best and worst scripts yourself
hand-reading the extremes of the score distribution

cap.1: A model wrote you 300 test questions. Some are great, some are broken. Reading them all is slow, so you hire a marker: another model, with a mark scheme.
cap.2: An LLM scorer grades each generated question against your rubric before it enters the dataset, and you drop those below a threshold. Pointed at model behaviour instead, the same machinery is an autorater.
cap.3: Model-graded scoring is the filter between cheap generation and an Inspect task. It returns as Inspect's model_graded_fact scorer and as the trusted monitor rating code suspiciousness in AI control.

cap.1: Tested against people, a strong model judge agreed with them over 80% of the time. But it favoured answers shown first, longer answers, and its own writing.
cap.2: Zheng et al. (MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, NeurIPS 2023): GPT-4 matched human preferences at over 80% agreement, about as often as two humans agree, and showed position, verbosity and self-enhancement bias.
cap.3: One mechanism behind all three: with nothing concrete to compare against, the judge grades what it can see. Fixes: swap order and average, length-matched anchors, no self-grading, reference-guided grading for maths.

chapters.name: Anchor the scale
chapters.title: an example rubric for a power-seeking question set
values: on topic, but the answer is obvious

cap.1: Give the marker a real mark scheme: say what a 0, a 50 and a 100 look like for your property, and show sample scripts, with a confident wrong one marked low.
cap.2: Fix a range (0 to 100 works) and anchor the endpoints and midpoint in your property's terms, not general adjectives. Few-shot scoring examples should include a confidently worded wrong one scored low.
cap.3: Anchors turn an open judgement into a comparison, which is what starves surface-feature bias. This rubric is illustrative; real anchors come from your own operational definition of the property.

parts.note: a tag the parser can find

cap.1: Make the marker write the comment before the mark. A mark given first is a snap judgement, and the comment then just makes excuses for it.
cap.2: Exercise: the grader returns an explanation, then an integer score wrapped in SCORE tags. Parse the tags, and count parse failures separately instead of slipping a default score into the data.
cap.3: ARENA's QCResponse carries explanation and score, so the number is conditioned on an argument. A sentinel score silently entering the distribution as if it were a judgement is worse than a biased judgement.

chapters.name: Confident and wrong
chapters.verdict: Read the top ten and bottom ten: if you disagree, fix the rubric, not the judge.

cap.1: Ask 'score this out of 100' and the marker rewards confidence: a wrong answer stated boldly beats a right one stated carefully. It's marking tone, not truth.
cap.2: With an unanchored scale the judge grades surface features: length, formatting, assertiveness. Anchor the scale, show a confident wrong example scored low, then hand-read the highest and lowest scores.
cap.3: Verbosity bias is the measured version; assertiveness rides the same mechanism, since confidence correlates with quality in the judge's training data. Asking for the number before the reason makes it worse.

chapters.name: What it can't see
chapters.title: which option carries the matching answer: expected, then found

cap.1: Every question passed the marker, yet 70% of the matching answers are Yes, so an always-Yes dummy scores 70%. The marker only ever saw one question at a time.
cap.2: Per-item scoring can't see set-level defects. Run balance checks beside the score statistics: count which option carries answer_matching_behavior and which categories dominate, and test an always-yes baseline.
cap.3: Yes-bias and category imbalance are properties of the joint distribution, invisible to any item-level grader. ARENA's summarize_results returns score statistics plus Counters over answer and category balance.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: The filter's habits become the eval's habits

cap.1: Evals are how we check what AI systems will do. The scorer decides which questions make the cut, so its habits quietly become the eval's habits.
cap.2: The same pattern grades model behaviour (autoraters), checks facts in Inspect (model_graded_fact) and rates code suspiciousness in AI control. All of them live or die on how the rubric is anchored.
cap.3: Model grading is licensed by human-level agreement and constrained by named biases. Treat the judge as an instrument: anchor it, audit the extremes, count parse failures, and check the set as a whole.

params.label: rubric anchoring (0 marks tone, 1 marks content)

curves.label: chance a question of quality x is kept
what you wanted: keep the good half

caption.1: Slide the anchoring. Near 0 the marker scores tone, and about half of what it keeps is junk whatever the bar. Near 1, the bar finally does what you meant.
caption.2: Toy scorer over 300 synthetic questions: score = a·quality + (1 − a)·polish. The orange curve is the chance a question of quality x survives. Try a = 0.2, then 0.9, with the bar at 0.5 and at 0.7.
caption.3: When the score loads on a feature unrelated to quality, a stricter bar mostly selects harder for that feature and wrecks recall. Anchors and few-shot examples raise a; reading the extremes by hand tells you where it sits.

where_else: Autoraters: the same machinery grading model behaviour in a study rather than dataset quality
Inspect's model_graded_fact scorer, used when a string match can't tell whether an answer contains the target fact
Trusted monitoring in AI control: a trusted model rating how suspicious another model's code looks
Pairwise LLM judging, as in MT-Bench, where position bias is handled by swapping the order and averaging

hamming.what: A language model grading each generated question against your written rubric, so that only those above a threshold enter the dataset.
hamming.when: Whenever there are too many generated items to read by hand, as with ARENA's 300-question eval sets.
hamming.why: It makes quality control scale, but a judge grades what it can see, so an unanchored rubric quietly turns your filter into a tone detector.

object.title: The tilting cliff
object.subtitle: A plateau of kept questions above a lowland of dropped ones; the rubric decides which way the cliff edge points.

cap.1: High ground is kept, low ground is dropped. Across: how good a question really is. Deep: how polished it sounds. The cliff edge is the marker's bar.
cap.2: A toy scorer: score = a·quality + (1 − a)·polish, kept if it clears threshold t. Height is a smoothed keep-or-drop decision over every mix of quality and polish.
cap.3: The keep region is a half-plane whose boundary a·x + (1 − a)·y = t rotates with a, the weight the judge puts on content rather than surface features.

cap.1: With a vague rubric, look from above: the edge runs almost along the quality axis, so polish decides. Polished junk is kept; plain good questions fall.
cap.2: At a = 0.2 the boundary depends mostly on polish. The filter is working hard, just on the wrong feature: a tone detector wearing a quality label.
cap.3: Boundary slope dy/dx = −a/(1 − a) = −0.25: nearly flat in quality, so the decision is almost independent of the property you care about.

cap.1: Now anchor the rubric. The cliff swings round until its edge runs along the polish axis: only quality decides. Junk drops, plain good questions stay.
cap.2: At a = 0.9 the boundary depends almost only on quality. Same threshold, same questions; the rubric changed which way the cliff points.
cap.3: Anchors and few-shot counter-examples move weight from surface features onto content: boundary slope −9, nearly perpendicular to the quality axis.

cap.1: Lower the bar and the plateau widens: more questions kept, including middling ones. The threshold sets how many; the anchoring sets which.
cap.2: Threshold and rubric are separate levers. t trades how many you keep against how strict you are; a decides what the strictness is about.
cap.3: Moving t translates the boundary; moving a rotates it. Precision depends on the rotation far more than on the translation when polish and quality are unrelated.

cap.1: With a vague rubric, raising the bar doesn't rescue you: only the most polished questions survive, and nearly every plain good one is thrown out.
cap.2: At a = 0.2 and t = 0.9 the filter keeps a thin, very polished sliver. A stricter bar on a badly anchored score just selects harder for tone.
cap.3: Tightening a threshold on a proxy concentrates selection on the proxy's dominant feature: Goodhart at dataset scale.

predict.q: Your grader scores a confidently worded wrong answer above a cautious correct one. What is the first fix?

options.t: Anchor the scale and add a confident-but-wrong example scored low
Switch to a bigger judge model

predict.why: With nothing concrete to compare against, the judge grades tone. Anchors and a demonstrated counter-example give it something real to compare.

predict.q: Why ask the grader for its explanation before the number?

options.t: So the score is conditioned on an argument, not rationalised afterwards
It makes the output easier to parse

predict.why: A number given first is a snap judgement; the explanation then justifies a score already committed to.

predict.q: Every item passes the scorer, yet an always-Yes dummy scores 70% on your set. What went wrong?

options.t: The matching answers are lopsided, which no per-item grader can see
The keep threshold is too low
The judge model is biased towards Yes

predict.why: Yes-bias is a property of the whole set. Run balance counts beside the score statistics, and keep an always-yes baseline as a control.

object.where: Anywhere a model grades at scale: dataset filters, autoraters, Inspect's model_graded_fact, trusted monitors in AI control.
